one_line_idea: SAM's output granularity (part vs whole) is a near-deterministic function of click position relative to the object's medial axis, not a reflection of genuine ambiguity resolution.

Box-prompt slack acts as an undocumented continuous scale prompt: SAM reads how loose a box is as a tolerance signal, so mask area inflates predictably with box dilation even when the object is unambiguous.
Although SAM encodes point sets symmetrically, PEFT-finetuned interactive variants develop click-order sensitivity, breaking the set-invariance contract users rely on.

Negative clicks are strictly weaker than positive clicks in SAM: removing an over-segmented region takes systematically more clicks than adding an equivalent under-segmented region, revealing an asymmetric prompt algebra.

Prompt-jitter robustness is a leading indicator of domain-shift robustness: PEFT-adapted SAMs lose click-jitter stability before their centroid-click accuracy drops, giving a label-free early-warning metric for over-adaptation.
Most objects contain interior adversarial click points where frozen SAM returns near-zero-IoU masks, and these failure points cluster along internal texture boundaries rather than being random.
Masks produced by SAM's automatic everything mode are frequently not reproducible by any single click, meaning automatic and interactive SAM are effectively two different segmenters sharing weights.

When box and point prompts conflict, SAM resolves the conflict by a fixed learned hierarchy rather than evidence weighting, and PEFT silently reorders that hierarchy, changing pipeline behavior without any accuracy metric noticing.

The click-to-mask map of SAM has measurable sub-pixel aliasing: masks can flip discontinuously between adjacent click pixels due to positional-encoding interpolation, defining an effective Lipschitz constant of promptable segmentation.

Because SAM rescales every image to a fixed input resolution, the same physical click has resolution-dependent semantics: click informativeness and effective precision degrade lawfully with source image size, an unmodeled shift for high-resolution domains.

LoRA adaptation of SAM to shifted domains mostly learns low-order intensity and color recalibration, not new shape priors: matched-histogram preprocessing recovers most of the LoRA gain without any weight updates.
Rank-1 LoRA is sufficient for modality-level adaptation of SAM, and everything above rank 1 fits annotation style rather than domain content, measurable by cross-annotator generalization.

Where LoRA is placed in SAM changes what is learned, not just how much: attention-projection LoRA learns spatial grouping changes while MLP LoRA learns appearance re-mapping, yielding qualitatively different error profiles at equal parameter count.

Decoder-only PEFT can match encoder PEFT for many domain shifts because the gap manifests as prompt-token-to-feature misalignment rather than feature deficiency, contradicting the default that the encoder must adapt.
Task-specific PEFT silently destroys SAM's ambiguity machinery: after adaptation, the three multimask outputs collapse toward one mask, removing a capability no downstream metric tracks.

Adapter-tuned SAM exhibits within-image interference: adaptation for target structures measurably degrades masks for untouched object categories present in the same images, a ripple effect invisible to target-only evaluation.

The sample-efficiency crossover between head-only tuning and LoRA is predictable before training from a frozen-feature similarity score, giving a decision rule for which PEFT to use at a given dataset size.

Bias-only tuning (BitFit-style) of SAM matches LoRA on texture- and intensity-shifted domains, implying that most claimed domain adaptation for segmentation is feature re-centering, not feature re-learning.

PEFT overfits to the prompt type used during adaptation: LoRA trained with box prompts degrades point-prompt performance on the same domain (and vice versa), violating the assumed prompt-agnosticism of adaptation.

Under sequential PEFT, promptability forgets faster than features: SAM adapted to domain B after domain A retains transferable features (linear probes stay strong) while interactive behavior on domain A collapses, locating forgetting in the prompt pathway.

Weight-space merging of independently trained domain LoRAs works unusually well for SAM (compared to classification adapters) because prompt conditioning absorbs cross-domain conflicts, making the merged model a testbed for when adapter arithmetic succeeds.

Visual prompt-token tuning (VPT-style) preserves SAM's everything-mode and zero-shot behavior far better than LoRA at equal target-domain accuracy, because appended tokens cannot rewrite spatial feature geometry.

SAM's predicted-IoU head is a mask-style critic, not an accuracy estimator: under domain shift its score tracks smoothness and compactness of the mask more than true IoU, which breaks every pipeline that uses the score for filtering.

judge_B.note: Load-bearing idea: A-025, A-086, A-091 all presuppose or contest the IoU-head score's meaning. Run A-023 first; its outcome reprices three other ideas.

one_line_idea: During PEFT, calibration of the IoU head collapses before mask quality does, so score-vs-truth divergence on a small probe set is an early-warning signal for harmful over-adaptation.

SAM's own score distribution is a free domain-shift detector: the shape of predicted-IoU histograms over grid prompts detects out-of-distribution imagery as well as dedicated feature-space OOD methods, at zero additional model cost.

SAM's ambiguity bottleneck is ranking, not generation: the correct mask is frequently among the three outputs but not top-ranked, so fixing selection (a tiny head) would harvest most of the oracle-vs-deployed gap.

Disagreement between SAM's stability score and its predicted IoU score is a label-error detector: pixels-cheap, model-free-of-extra-training, and usable to audit ground truth in segmentation datasets.

SAM's three multimask outputs are not diverse hypotheses but a hard-coded scale quantization (part, object, group), which predicts a specific failure family on structures without hierarchical scale organization.

Recalibrating only SAM's IoU head on a shifted domain (freezing all mask-producing weights) recovers a large fraction of practical pipeline performance, because deployed loss is dominated by wrong mask selection and wrong filtering thresholds.
Variance across SAM's internal token-to-image attention maps localizes boundary errors: an unused, training-free per-pixel uncertainty map already exists inside the decoder.

SAM encoder features are excellent boundary features but poor semantic features, and the two qualities anti-correlate across layers, refuting the assumption that a segmentation foundation model is a general visual foundation model.

The layer-wise need for adaptation in SAM is U-shaped: earliest and final encoder layers require updates while the middle two-thirds are domain-universal, contradicting both adapt-everything and adapt-last-layers defaults.

SAM's windowed-attention design leaves a grid fingerprint: under domain shift, segmentation errors cluster along the window boundaries of the ViT, an architecture-induced spatial artifact nobody audits for.

judge_B.note: Anomaly: architecture-fingerprint via Fourier analysis of aggregate error maps; inference-only, hours, unusual and decisive either way.

one_line_idea: Despite being trained to find boundaries, SAM remains texture-biased in the cue-conflict sense: when shape and texture disagree, its groupings follow texture, showing that segmentation training does not confer shape bias.

Token-norm inflation under domain shift maps where adaptation is needed: per-layer feature-norm statistics on unlabeled target images predict the optimal LoRA placement, enabling data-driven adapter allocation without any labels.

Aspect-ratio distortion from SAM's square-padded resizing is a first-order hidden failure source for thin elongated structures, rivaling texture shift in damage but fixable by inference-time letterboxing choices alone.

SAM is unusually sensitive to JPEG and resampling artifacts because SA-1B consisted of high-quality licensed photography, making compression level an unmodeled domain axis that hits SAM harder than supervised baselines.

SAM's encoder exhibits high-norm outlier tokens (register-like sinks), and their spatial positions correlate with mask leakage errors, linking a known ViT pathology to concrete segmentation failures for the first time.

The two-layer mask decoder, not the encoder, is the binding constraint for dense thin structures: deepening only the decoder (keeping the encoder frozen) recovers vessel- and crack-like segmentation that encoder PEFT cannot, at a fraction of the parameters.

SAM's mask tokens are overloaded scale-generalists: forcing token specialization by object scale (a handful of scale-conditioned output tokens) tests whether token capacity, not feature quality, limits small-object segmentation.

SAM has a constant systematic boundary offset (not proportional jitter) traceable to its 4x upsampling path, which means a universal sub-pixel correction could improve every SAM output at zero model cost.

judge_B.note: One of the cleanest cheap kills in the whole wave: synthetic exact boundaries, signed offset histogram, an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Promptable segmentation cannot express relationally-defined regions (the gap between two objects, the part of A occluded by B), a representational blind spot of prompt-as-locator interfaces that no amount of PEFT fixes.

The hypernetwork MLP mapping mask tokens to dynamic convolution weights in SAM is effectively linear: distilling it to a linear map costs almost nothing, revealing that the decoder's expressive component is placed where expressivity is not used.

Prompt tokens dilute output tokens in decoder self-attention: SAM's accuracy degradation with many clicks is an attention-budget artifact with a predictable functional form, fixable by attention masking rather than retraining.

Encoder-side PEFT breaks an implicit encoder-decoder contract in SAM: feature drift makes the frozen decoder's cross-attention read features it was never calibrated for, and a contract-violation metric predicts when joint (vs encoder-only) tuning is required.

SAM's decoder cannot represent holes below a scale threshold: mask topology is systematically simplified (genus reduced) as hole size shrinks, defining a topological failure family with a measurable critical scale.

SAM2's memory bank induces confirmation bias: early mask errors are written to memory and then re-read as evidence, making per-object error growth superlinear after occlusions in a way promptless re-initialization would avoid.

SAM2's object memory encodes appearance rather than identity: repeated similar objects (twins, uniform players, identical parts) cause identity swaps at rates predictable from appearance similarity alone, exposing the absence of spatiotemporal identity binding.

Video training regressed SAM2's single-image behavior in specific structure families relative to SAM1 (a capability trade nobody has mapped), so image-mode users may be silently better served by the older model.

SAM2 has a hard forgetting horizon set by its memory capacity: reacquisition probability after occlusion collapses at a critical occlusion duration (a cliff, not a slope), and the cliff location is a fixed architectural constant rather than content-dependent.

For video domain shift, adapting only SAM2's memory-attention layers beats adapting the image encoder at equal parameter budget: domain gap in video lives in temporal association, not appearance encoding.

SAM2's occlusion prediction is a motion-prior guess, not an evidence-based judgment: it infers disappearance from motion patterns rather than from what pixels show, failing lawfully on static occlusions and motionless disappearances.

SAM2 has a preferred temporal sampling rate: tracking accuracy is non-monotone in frame rate, peaking near training-video statistics, so both slowing down and speeding up input degrades it, contrary to the assumption that more frames never hurt.

Propagation in SAM2 is temporally asymmetric beyond content effects: propagating a middle-frame prompt backward is systematically worse than forward, revealing an architectural arrow of time that batch (offline) video adaptation should exploit or repair.

Adapting SAM2 on domain video corrupts its image-mode promptability faster than adapting SAM1 on matched images does, because gradients through memory attention couple the static pathway to temporal objectives, making video PEFT uniquely forgetting-prone.

Model-in-the-loop data generation gave SAM a mask-style monoculture: SA-1B's semi-automatic pipeline filtered out messy, low-compactness masks, so SAM inherits a compactness prior that is a data-flywheel artifact, not a property of the visual world.

SAM carries a photographic-composition prior: mask quality for identical content varies with its position in the frame (center and rule-of-thirds hotspots), an artifact of professional photography in SA-1B that surveillance and industrial imagery violates wholesale.

judge_B.note: Kept as primary of the photographic-canon-prior pair on cost grounds (see merge note on A-061; direction disagrees with Judge A).

one_line_idea: Class-agnostic training left latent semantics in SAM: its masks snap to semantic category boundaries even when low-level evidence contradicts them, so SAM is a covert semantic segmenter whose hidden classes bias supposedly geometry-only outputs.

SAM's part-vs-whole ambiguity resolution is anchored to SA-1B's mask-size distribution: when object-to-image size ratios leave the training regime, granularity choices become systematically biased (macro shots yield parts, distant shots yield groups) independent of prompt intent.

Guideline archaeology: SAM's handling of pathological cases (wires, fences, reflections, transparent objects) encodes recoverable traces of SA-1B annotation-guideline decisions, showing that foundation models memorize policy, not just imagery.

SA-1B's grid-prompt generation left a periodic spatial fingerprint in SAM: averaged over many images, mask-probability and mask-seed statistics show energy at the generation grid frequency, an unnoticed artifact coupling dataset construction to model prior.

Benchmark mIoU anti-correlates with interactive usability across PEFT methods: adapters that win static benchmarks require more correction clicks in deployment because they trade prompt responsiveness for prompt-independent priors.
Boundary metrics conflate constant offset with jitter: decomposing boundary error into bias and variance components changes which PEFT method wins, because methods differ in which component they fix.

Centroid-click evaluation is a lucky-prompt protocol: model rankings among adapted SAMs invert under prompt distributions sampled from real user behavior, because centroid clicks are systematically easier than human clicks.

judge_B.note: Co-collect human clicks once for A-069 and A-092; one 300-500 object click corpus serves both.

one_line_idea: SAM's failures are bimodal (near-perfect or catastrophic), so mean metrics track the mixture weight rather than segmentation quality, and PEFT methods should be compared by failure-rate curves instead of averages.

Cross-paper PEFT-for-SAM comparisons are confounded by prompt-simulation policy more than by method: a controlled re-implementation shows the prompt protocol explains more ranking variance than the adaptation technique being advertised.

Corruption robustness of SAM is prompt-type dependent in a structured way (boxes resist blur, points resist occlusion, and vice versa fails), so prompt choice is a free robustness lever no pipeline currently exploits.

Universal adversarial prompt perturbations exist: a single learned pixel-offset field applied to any user click (imperceptible at UI level) collapses SAM's masks across images, exposing prompt space as an unsecured attack surface cheaper than image attacks.

judge_B.note: KEEP-flagged in disagreement with Judge A (who killed as permutation): the staged kill is exemplary - per-image worst-case bound first, universal field only if that survives. Cheap, decisive, but low novelty priority.

one_line_idea: PEFT concentrates adversarial vulnerability: LoRA-adapted SAM is easier to attack than either frozen SAM or fully fine-tuned SAM, because low-rank updates create a small, findable subspace whose manipulation controls the whole adapted behavior.

SAM's low-contrast failures are threshold failures, not perception failures: under fog or dim light the logit landscape preserves the object (rank order intact) but the fixed binarization threshold misplaces the boundary, so an input-conditional threshold fixes fog for free.

Geometry-only prompting makes SAM structurally immune to typographic and semantic-patch attacks that fool text-conditioned segmenters, a security advantage of coordinate interfaces that quantifies the robustness cost of language conditioning.

SAM's transferability to a new domain is predicted by that domain's mid-frequency spectral content: band-pass ablation shows SAM relies on a specific spatial-frequency band, and domains missing it (ultrasound speckle, low-detail thermal) fail regardless of semantic simplicity.

SAM flips inconsistently between modal (visible-region) and amodal (completed-object) segmentation depending on prompt position relative to an occluder, an unacknowledged mode ambiguity that makes its outputs unreliable as either kind of ground truth.

Distillation kills ambiguity first: efficient SAM students match teacher mIoU while losing most of the teacher's hypothesis-space structure (multimask diversity, granularity control), because distillation targets the argmax mask, not the distribution over valid masks.

Distilled students fail on a strict superset of teacher failures: compression does not trade failure regions but nests them, so teacher-side failure prediction transfers to students for free, enabling cheap cascade designs.

Feature-space distillation preserves prompt responsiveness while output-space distillation destroys it: two certified-equivalent compression routes produce behaviorally different interactive models, and the difference is invisible to standard benchmarks.

Quantization is prompt-type biased: INT8 SAM loses point-prompt accuracy well before box-prompt accuracy, because sparse point information rides small activations that quantization noise drowns, making current quantization certifications misleading for interactive use.

Token merging and pruning for SAM encoders selectively destroys thin and small structures long before average metrics move, because merging criteria based on feature similarity preferentially eliminate the minority tokens carrying rare-structure evidence.

The IoU head is a free adapter router: selecting which domain LoRA to apply per image by comparing SAM's own predicted-score distributions under each adapter beats both single adapters and weight merging, with zero additional trained parameters.

judge_B.note: KEEP-flagged in disagreement with Judge A: one-afternoon kill, and it is in designed tension with A-023 (if the score is a style critic, score-routing should fail in a diagnostic way).

one_line_idea: Catastrophic remembering: narrow-domain PEFT resurrects pretraining biases that SAM's final training had suppressed (texture leakage, compact-mask preference), so adaptation can move a model backward along its own training history, not just away from it.

Interference between simultaneously-composed LoRAs is predicted by principal angles between their update subspaces: a five-minute weight-space measurement forecasts whether two adapters can be stacked, replacing trial-and-error composition.

Domain shifts share low-rank structure: one shared LoRA trained jointly on N diverse domains matches N separate LoRAs at one-Nth the parameters, implying that adaptation learns a common shift-correction operator rather than N unrelated fixes.

Self-training SAM on its own confident masks converges to degenerate over-smooth segmentation because the confidence signal is style-biased (idea 023): the obvious test-time adaptation baseline is predicted to fail in a specific, diagnosable way.

Click-policy shift is a hidden domain gap: SAM was trained on simulator clicks (error-region centers), humans click salient interiors and high-contrast landmarks, and this policy mismatch accounts for a measurable slice of real-world underperformance relative to benchmarks.

judge_B.note: Shares the human-click corpus with A-069.

one_line_idea: Interactive correction has oscillation modes: correcting one region creates errors elsewhere with probability that grows with adaptation strength, so heavily adapted SAMs exhibit whack-a-mole dynamics that make some targets uncorrectable in finite clicks.

The model's best click is not where humans click: a gradient-derived where-to-click advisor (computed from SAM's own sensitivity) increases per-click information and cuts annotation time, revealing that human click intuitions are miscalibrated to the model's actual decision geometry.

Fine-tuning on accumulated user corrections personalizes toward the user's annotation style rather than toward accuracy: correction-trained models drift measurably toward individual annotator idiosyncrasies, conflating personalization with improvement.

Prompt reuse across near-duplicate images fails silently at a predictable rate: prompts transferred between adjacent video frames or repeated product shots produce degraded masks without degraded confidence, defining an unstudied reliability metric (prompt transferability) for promptable models.

Resolution adaptation is a positional-encoding problem, not a feature problem: tuning only SAM's positional embeddings (all other weights frozen) recovers most of the gain that high-resolution fine-tuning provides, isolating where resolution knowledge lives.

PEFT under a fixed prompt protocol turns SAM into a prompt-ignoring semantic segmenter: adapted models' outputs become nearly invariant to prompt content, meaning many published adapted-SAM results are really measuring a learned semantic prior wearing a promptable interface.

For non-RGB modalities, a tiny learned input stem beats the standard channel-inflation trick: freezing all of SAM and learning only a 1x1 modality-to-pseudo-RGB projection outperforms replicating RGB weights across channels, showing the modality gap lives at the input interface.

Loss choice shapes mask topology more than architecture choice: the focal-plus-dice convention in SAM adaptation imposes a measurable bias toward simply-connected masks, an ignored confound that may explain topology-related conclusions across the PEFT literature.

Pseudo-label bias amplification law: students trained on SAM everything-mode outputs inherit its anti-small, anti-thin biases amplified by a measurable factor, so each generation of SAM-labeled training data drifts further from reality in a predictable direction.
Binary masks are a category error for smoke: segmentation error concentrates in a penumbra band that tracks optical thickness, not annotation noise.
Smoke annotators implicitly choose a personal opacity threshold, so inter-annotator disagreement is predictable from local contrast alone.
Boundary-aware losses presuppose that boundaries exist; on amorphous classes they may actively harm learning.
The extent of a fire region in an image is partly a camera property: predictions may track exposure settings more than physical fire size.
Supervising with soft alpha mattes instead of binary masks changes what the encoder learns, not just what the head outputs.
Models inherit a blob prior from annotators and systematically erase the fractal, multi-connected fine structure of real smoke.
Fixing an operational opacity threshold may collapse expert disagreement about smoke extent, showing the ambiguity is definitional, not perceptual.
Inside a transparent object, foundation-model features may encode the background seen through it better than the object itself.
Transparent-object segmentation may run almost entirely on contour and context, collapsing disproportionately when the silhouette is occluded.
Do segmentation models use refraction at all? Rendered index-of-refraction ablations can measure it directly.
Specular highlights may be the load-bearing shortcut for glass detection; cross-polarized imagery could collapse current models.
Depth foundation models place glass at the background depth; segmentation models sharing those backbones may inherit the glass-invisible prior.
Glass and smoke fail differently: geometric boundaries with weak photometrics jitter, photometric gradients without geometry smear; a two-axis failure taxonomy is testable.

judge_B.note: Kept as primary over B-089 (reverse of Judge A): displacement-statistics separability is a falsifiable instrument; taxonomy discovery is its output, not a separate testable claim.

one_line_idea: Static single-image transparent-object segmentation may sit near an information-theoretic ceiling that humans also cannot beat without motion.
Training on randomly sampled single raters versus the majority vote may not add noise but shift boundary placement in a consistent direction.
The direction of systematic over- or under-segmentation may be set by the loss function, not the data, in a predictable size-dependent way.
Model uncertainty maps may fail to correlate with where human experts actually disagree, because they measure the wrong kind of doubt.
Predicting rater-percentile contours (p10, p50, p90) as explicit nested targets, and testing when nesting is even valid.
Models may learn institution-specific contouring conventions so strongly that the annotating institution is decodable from predicted masks alone.
Ambiguous pixels and difficult pixels are different populations, possibly anti-correlated, and current methods conflate them.
Lesion-level detection ranking versus voxel-overlap ranking: the field may be selecting architectures that reliably miss small lesions.
Boundary voxels are physical mixtures (partial volume): regressing mixture fractions may beat classification and match physics on phantoms.
Promptable segmentation foundation models may exhibit a measurable snapping field: masks jump to the nearest high-contrast contour regardless of prompt intent on amorphous targets.

judge_B.note: Shares click-response-field tooling with A-001/A-006/A-009; build the grid-sweep harness once.

one_line_idea: Prompt-output variance as a free ambiguity detector: the spread of masks under prompt jitter may track true target ambiguity.
A gradient snapping coefficient: quantifying how strongly mask decoders relocate semantic boundaries onto photometric gradients.
Foundation-model failure on hard domains may be predictable from the mismatch between target scale statistics and pretraining object-scale priors.
Scaling pretraining data may asymptote for transparency and smoke because the missing ingredient is label ontology, not pixels.
Text-prompted segmentation may ground count nouns better than mass nouns, disadvantaging smoke, fluid, and tissue categories linguistically.
A linear-separability audit of frozen foundation features across hard domains: is the deficit in the features or in the decoders?
Under ambiguity, foundation segmenters may output confident all-or-nothing masks with a detectable bimodal signature instead of graded responses.
IoU on soft-boundary targets mostly measures whether the model guessed the annotator's threshold, not whether it perceived the medium.
Boundary-quality metrics on fractal boundaries may rank mask-smoothing hyperparameters, not models.
Metric forensics: the training loss may leave identifiable morphological fingerprints in predicted masks.
Test downstream utility directly: matting-style perceptual error may predict task usefulness of smoke masks better than IoU does.
Fixed-threshold evaluation penalizes calibrated soft predictions: models honest about ambiguity may score worse than overconfident ones.
Smoke segmenters may be global haze-statistics detectors: histogram manipulations could flip predictions with local structure fixed.
Fire segmentation may depend on sensor saturation: HDR imagery without clipped pixels could break current models.
When intensity and shape cues conflict in medical images, models may follow intensity even where shape says otherwise; the conflict point is measurable.
Smoke may be predicted wherever fire context appears: pasting fire-adjacent context into clean scenes could conjure phantom smoke masks.
Video-compression artifacts may be a learned smoke cue: recompression could move masks more than scene changes do.
Texture-shape bias may be amplified at segmentation boundaries: per-pixel stylization tests could show boundary decisions are texture-driven where shape should rule.
Single-frame smoke benchmarks may leak motion information through blur signatures, inflating reported single-image capability.
Smoke versus steam versus fog: current models may be undifferentiated haze detectors, and a confusability audit would expose the semantic emptiness.
Pixelwise calibration can be perfect while extent estimates are wildly miscalibrated, because dense errors are spatially correlated; extent-level calibration is the missing target.

judge_B.note: Top cheap-kill of shard B uncertainty cluster: temperature-scale once, measure realized area-interval coverage in hours.

one_line_idea: On hard domains, feature-space distance to training data may predict errors better than the model's own confidence does.
Deep ensembles may agree on the same wrong crisp boundary instead of spanning plausible contours, underestimating ambiguity in a systematic direction.
Naive pixelwise conformal prediction for masks may deliver nominal marginal coverage while structure-level coverage is near zero.
Boundary ambiguity wants soft maps; topological ambiguity wants mask sets: a dissociation experiment could establish the representation-ambiguity matching law.
Confidence-correctness correlation may invert on transparent objects: models could be most confident exactly where glass fools them.
Beer-Lambert attenuation suggests log-transmittance, not alpha, as the natural regression target for smoke; conditioning of the loss landscape may differ measurably.
Thin and thick smoke are different physical regimes (single versus multiple scattering); training data may cover one and models may silently fail on the other.
Fire is an emitter, not a reflector: emissive regions violate learned shading priors, and characteristic halo errors around flames may be the fingerprint.
Polarization may carry the signal RGB lacks for glass and smoke: small polarization probes could beat large RGB foundation models, proving an information gap rather than a model gap.

judge_B.note: Sharp hypothesis but hardware-gated (polarimetric camera); keep at low wave priority until hardware access is confirmed.

one_line_idea: Modeling the scanner's point-spread function inside the label likelihood may correct a systematic boundary bias that no amount of data can fix.
Smoke, fog, and haze are points in one scattering-parameter space: regressing physical parameters might generalize where classification fundamentally cannot.
Smoke casts shadows that encode its optical thickness; models likely ignore this free evidence, and shadow-occlusion counterfactuals can prove it.
Smoke is a process, not an object: tiny temporal models may beat huge single-frame foundation models at equal compute because the signal lives in dynamics.
Combustion imposes characteristic flicker dynamics on flames; frame-trained models cannot represent them, and the deficit is measurable as a specific hard-negative failure.
If smoke-extent ambiguity is structured rather than noisy, temporal averaging of predictions will not shrink it at the rate independent noise predicts; the deviation measures ambiguity structure.
Optical-flow-based pseudo-labeling breaks on participating media: flow tracks the background through smoke, making motion supervision anti-correlated with the medium.
Predicting spread-rate fields instead of extent masks: the derivative of the process may be more annotator-stable and decision-relevant than its instantaneous state.
Object-permanence priors in video models may actively harm dissipating-target tracking: memory mechanisms could hold onto smoke that no longer exists.
Event cameras may separate real flames from reflections of flames by capturing combustion microdynamics invisible at standard frame rates.

judge_B.note: Anomaly, hardware-gated (event camera). The one-afternoon candle/mirror pilot is the cheapest version; do not scale before it.

one_line_idea: Longitudinal context may collapse margin ambiguity in medical segmentation: growth direction could disambiguate boundaries that single scans cannot.

judge_B.note: Expert-gated (radiologist raters, longitudinal data). Keep but expect this to be blocked for this project; flag for consolidator.

one_line_idea: A fixed two-layer decomposition (medium plus background) may resolve most single-label errors in scenes with participating media, measuring the representational ceiling of flat segmentation.
Boundary ambiguity may be low-dimensional in signed-distance space: rater variation could compress to a few modes, enabling compact ambiguity representations.
Occupancy and opacity are conflated in smoke labels: annotators answer different questions on different pixels, and decomposing the two could resolve apparent label inconsistency.
Decoder upsampling architecture may impose a high-frequency prior that actively fights soft-boundary targets; frequency-response analysis of decoders could expose it.
Patch tokenization may quantize extent estimates in patch-size units on low-contrast boundaries, leaving a periodic fingerprint in error histograms.
Partial coverage and uncertainty are confounded in soft masks: a probability of one half can mean half-covered or fully-unknown, and the two need different downstream actions.
Query-based mask decoders presuppose countable instances; on uncountable media they may fragment continua into phantom instances with a measurable signature.
Predicting the level-set family instead of one mask: supervising all thresholds of a soft target simultaneously may regularize amorphous learning better than any single-threshold label.
The sim-to-real gap for smoke may concentrate in the thin-smoke regime where renderers approximate scattering most aggressively, making synthetic data mis-teach exactly the hard cases.
Sparse physical sensor labels (particulate, thermal) may beat dense human labels per unit cost for training calibrated smoke extent models.

judge_B.note: Fast version is runnable with public paired thermal-visible wildfire footage; the instrumented-release full version is a funded-lab experiment.

one_line_idea: Asking annotators for explicit dont-know bands may buy more calibration per annotation dollar than collecting more raters.
A measurable share of cross-site medical performance drop may be label-convention shift, isolable by re-contouring a subset under a unified protocol.
Active learning in ambiguous domains may spend its budget on irreducibly ambiguous pixels; separating ambiguity from epistemic uncertainty could double acquisition efficiency.
Copy-paste augmentation is physically invalid for participating media: pasted smoke without recomputed attenuation may teach models compositing artifacts as the cue.
Ambiguity-type transfer may beat domain-appearance transfer: training on smoke might help infiltrative tumor margins more than training on crisp tumors does.
Hard-domain benchmarks may be approaching label-entropy floors: an estimable irreducibility bound could separate real headroom from noise-chasing.
A shared learned contrast operator may underlie failures across glass, smoke, and lesions: adversarial contrast perturbations might transfer across all three domains.
Models may fail differently from humans on hard domains in a complementary way, implying human-model teams have more headroom here than anywhere else.
Partitioning benchmark error into information-absent, information-unused, and definition-absent components: a measurement protocol for what kind of hard each hard case is.

judge_B.note: High-payoff but protocol-heavy and vague as stated; recommend piloting the three bounds on ONE domain and twenty cases before any commitment.

one_line_idea: Distribution-matching evaluation: a large share of persistent hard-domain errors might be re-scored as acceptable answers under the rater distribution, changing what counts as progress.
Fixed-bin expected calibration error systematically misranks vision foundation models compared to debiased or binning-free calibration estimators.
In-distribution calibration of vision foundation models carries near-zero information about their calibration under distribution shift.
Full fine-tuning of vision foundation models improves in-distribution accuracy while systematically destroying calibration transferability relative to linear probing.

Verbalized confidence from multimodal vision-language models is systematically less reliable than their own token-level log-probabilities on visual questions, contradicting the intuition that self-reports add information.
Aggregate calibration hides severe tail-class miscalibration: vision foundation models that look calibrated on average are strongly overconfident exactly on rare classes.
Post-hoc calibration methods evaluated on held-out splits of the same distribution overstate their value because the fitted correction does not transfer across datasets.
A measurable share of apparent overconfidence in vision foundation models is actually test-label error, and models are better calibrated with respect to corrected labels.
Calibration evaluation for detection and segmentation is ill-defined as currently practiced because the confidence scores are ranking scores, not probabilities of any explicit event.
Ensembles of vision foundation models improve calibration mostly by uniformly shrinking confidence rather than by improving the ranking of which inputs are risky.
The epistemic-aleatoric uncertainty decomposition reported for vision models is not identifiable in practice: interventions designed to change one component move both estimates.
Marginal coverage claims of conformal prediction on vision benchmarks conceal severe conditional coverage failures under realistic covariate shift.
Standard out-of-distribution detection benchmarks are largely solvable by trivial low-level statistics, so reported method rankings measure benchmark artifacts.
Uncertainty-method rankings established on small networks and datasets invert at foundation scale, so the field's canonical conclusions may not transfer to the models people actually deploy.
Test-time-augmentation-based uncertainty mostly measures a model's augmentation sensitivity, not its predictive uncertainty, and the two decouple under simple interventions.
For multimodal models, answer instability across paraphrased visual prompts predicts errors better than the model's own internal confidence signals.
Error-detection AUROC as the standard uncertainty metric structurally favors accurate models, so uncertainty leaderboards partly re-measure accuracy.
Contamination of vision benchmarks by web-scale pretraining is systematically underestimated because deduplication tools detect pixel duplicates but not semantic duplicates of the same scene.

Zero-shot performance of vision foundation models is mostly seen-shot: accuracy stratified by similarity to pretraining data reveals the claimed generalization is concentrated where near-training content exists.
Annotation error rates in flagship vision test sets exceed the score gaps separating leading foundation models, so leaderboard order among top models is not measurable with current labels.
Val and test splits of legacy vision benchmarks are non-iid due to photographer, session, and source-page leakage, inflating scores relative to honest disjoint splits.
Synthetic corruption benchmarks poorly predict degradation on real-world image quality problems, so corruption-robustness scores are a misleading proxy for deployment robustness.
Benchmark aging is real: category semantics and visual distributions drift over time, so accuracy on decade-old test sets overstates accuracy on the same nominal task today.
Adaptive overfitting to reused test sets is measurable in the foundation-model era: models released later gain more on the canonical test set than on fresh replicas, controlling for capability.
General-purpose vision benchmarks embed demographic and geographic confounds that make aggregate scores unrepresentative and cross-model comparisons unstable across subpopulations.
Any fixed-feature-space distance metric for generative image evaluation is structurally gameable, and an adversarial-sensitivity audit should accompany every reported score.
Zero-shot retrieval recall correlates poorly with the end-task utility of embeddings inside retrieval-augmented multimodal pipelines.
Multi-task benchmark suite rankings are unstable under reasonable task reweighting, so suite-level leaderboards encode arbitrary editorial weight choices.
Repeated-sampling metrics for multimodal generation conflate output diversity with capability, crediting models for stochastic variety rather than reliability.
Micro-averaged accuracy hides that foundation-model progress is concentrated on frequent classes, and macro-averaged evaluation shows much flatter progress curves.
Uncontrolled prompt-engineering budgets act as hidden compute in zero-shot comparisons, and equalizing prompt-search effort shrinks or reverses claimed model gaps.
Linear-probe evaluation encodes a linearity assumption about representation quality, and shallow nonlinear probes rerank vision backbones, undermining probe-based pretraining conclusions.
Few-shot evaluation variance across support-set draws exceeds the model gaps typically reported, making single-draw few-shot comparisons close to meaningless.
Frozen-backbone comparisons are confounded by head architecture and head-training recipes, and standardizing heads changes which backbone wins.
Zero-shot classification rankings are unstable under synonym substitution of class names, revealing that benchmark-specific wording quietly advantages some models.
Random-seed variance in fine-tuning is large enough that many claimed state-of-the-art improvements at foundation scale are single-seed lottery wins.
Scaling up vision models does not improve calibration under distribution shift beyond what improved accuracy mechanically implies: a negative result about scale as an uncertainty cure.

judge_B.note: Cheapest sharp test in the negative-results cluster: public scale ladders, cached logits, accuracy-controlled regression in a day.

one_line_idea: Chain-of-thought prompting yields no genuine gain on visual reasoning benchmarks once answer-format effects and extra-token compute are controlled: a null result behind a popular technique.
Knowledge distillation from large vision foundation models transfers little beyond what label smoothing and better targets provide: a dark-knowledge null at foundation scale.
Feature-space augmentation and mixing methods that helped small-scale training deliver no measurable benefit when fine-tuning foundation backbones: a scale-dependent null.

Synthetic training images from generative models improve downstream benchmarks mainly when the test set shares the generator's stylistic biases, and gains evaporate on independently sourced test data.
Human-level performance claims in vision rest on weak human baselines, and expert or incentive-aligned human evaluation reopens the human-machine gap on several solved tasks.
Models beating human accuracy on benchmarks are often just out-predicting annotator disagreement: agreement-ceiling analysis reframes superhuman claims as majority-vote overfitting.

Ground truth is instruction-dependent: re-annotating the same images under different but equally reasonable instructions shifts model rankings, exposing benchmark truth as one convention among several.

Model-assisted annotation has quietly contaminated ground truth: benchmarks labeled with model-in-the-loop pipelines are biased toward the model families used, inflating those families' measured performance.
Quality-control gold questions bias test sets toward the unambiguous, so benchmarks systematically exclude the hard cases and overstate deployable accuracy.
Vision-language models used as judges of visual outputs exhibit self-preference and family-preference biases large enough to corrupt model comparisons that rely on them.

Annotation-vendor ecosystems create test-set leakage paths that deduplication cannot see: the same worker pools and internal guideline documents touch both training-data production and benchmark creation.

judge_B.note: Anomaly kept with a warning: vendor-provenance data is rarely public; narrow to datasets with documented annotation origins or this is unrunnable.

one_line_idea: A field-wide bootstrap audit of vision benchmark deltas: a large fraction of published improvements are within test-set resampling noise once paired item-level uncertainty is computed.

Leaderboards inflate apparent state-of-the-art through selection: the expected maximum over many noisy submissions exceeds true best performance, and the bias is quantifiable from submission statistics.
The vision benchmark ecosystem has low effective dimensionality: most benchmarks rank models nearly identically, so new benchmarks add publication events but little measurement information.
The same checkpoint scores materially differently across popular evaluation harnesses, and harness variance is an unbudgeted error term in every cross-paper comparison.
Silent test-informed model selection is endemic: development practices leak test-set signal into checkpoint choice, and a leakage-audit protocol can measure the resulting inflation.

judge_B.note: KEEP in disagreement with Judge A: the controlled dev-loop is the causal version of C-032's observational regression and is cheap; keep both, they triangulate.

one_line_idea: Published ablation tables systematically overstate component importance because ablations are run once, at one scale, on one seed: a variance-aware re-ablation study.

Effective-robustness analysis via linear fits on accuracy scatter plots breaks down near the accuracy ceiling, and conclusions about which interventions confer robustness flip under ceiling-aware models.

Distribution-shift benchmarks conflate multiple shift types into single scores, and factorizing shifts reveals that models robust on the benchmark are robust to only some factors deployments care about.
Fixed-epsilon adversarial evaluation is incomparable across models with different preprocessing and native resolutions, making cross-model robustness tables silently inconsistent.

Corruption-robustness gains from augmentation research are substantially overfitting to the benchmark's corruption menu, and generalization to held-out corruption families is much weaker than reported averages suggest.
Vision models certified robust by standard suites fail on temporal shift: robustness leaderboard leaders lose their advantage on data collected years after their training cutoffs.
Spurious-correlation benchmarks contain their own meta-spurious cues: models can score well on debiasing tests by exploiting artifacts of how the tests were constructed.
Certified-robustness guarantees do not predict empirical security under realistic attacks: certification radius and practical attack success are weakly related across defended models.
Object-hallucination benchmarks for captioning models measure language co-occurrence priors more than visual grounding, and a blind-model control quantifies exactly how much.

Visual-grounding scores of multimodal models collapse under image-swap consistency tests: models answer identically when the image is replaced, exposing text-shortcut reliance the benchmarks never check.
Reported multimodal reasoning gains on text-rich benchmarks are mostly optical-character-recognition gains in disguise, separable by transcribed-input ablations.
Chart and diagram question-answering benchmarks are contaminated by template reuse: finite generator templates make test items predictable from training exposure, inflating scores.

judge_B.note: KEEP in disagreement with Judge A: template re-rendering is a distinct falsification design (controlled counterfactual), not another blind baseline.

one_line_idea: Video-understanding benchmarks remain largely solvable from one or a few frames even for the newest foundation models, so temporal-understanding claims are still uncertified.
Safety evaluations of multimodal models measure refusal-style pattern matching rather than harm-relevant capability, and style-normalized re-evaluation reorders safety leaderboards.

The assumption that higher pretraining data quality uniformly improves downstream performance is wrong: quality filtering helps some downstream tasks while measurably hurting others, and the trade-off is hidden by suite averages.

English-centric class names and prompts are an ignored evaluation assumption: multilingual re-evaluation of zero-shot vision models changes rankings and reveals language-dependent capability profiles.
